body: I believe this is a bug actually.  According to [the RFC](http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec19.html), it should just be a string or a quoted string.
I believe the decoder is also affected by this issue.  Assigning to @fredericBregier for fundamental fixes.

I agree, don't know/remember why this was this way...
I am unable at least before 1 week to make the necessary changes on both versions. So if urgent, no issue if someone else takes it.

Thanks for looking into this.

Actually there is another potential issue. It's easier to work around it, but still...

The multipart encoder always adds a line `Content-Type: charset=UTF-8` to all simple attribute fields, like this:

``` text
--5d122409bcced0a9
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="t"
Content-Type: charset=UTF-8

hw31z8EDqciuwRuqPKFWNKk_
--5d122409bcced0a9
```

Note that there is no real content-type/subtype specified (or necessary). Only the (default) encoding is provided.
Many 3rd party web applications can handle this, they are probably ignoring the Content-Type line. But some are not, they complain about invalid content.

The only way to avoid the rendering of the "Content-Type" line is by setting the charset property of the HttpData element to null. Unfortunately, the standard setter doen't allow this. And the multipart decoder will always set the charset property to the default value (UTF-8). So by first reading and then writing a POST multipart message, there is no straight forward way to avoid the "Content-Type" line in the rendered output.

I am still not able to work on it, but if @39tybs wants to propose his own proposal, no issue for me.

Note on the last comment, it is mandatory to specified the Content-Type since the attributes are encoded using the default charset given as parameter to the encoder constructor (default being UTF-8 if not explicitely specified).

Not giving this information could lead to misdecoding part on server/client side. This is not an option, but a garantee to be correctly decoded.
If you do not specify this, then how will you manage UTF-8 vs ASCII vs ISO-8859-1 vs ... ?

Now regarding the issue about the decoder, the decoder is created with a charset (default being UTF-8) and this default is only used in case:
1) there is not multipart, so only Body => no ContentType at all so default is used
2) there is a multipart, but ContentType is not defined, then default is used
3) there is a multipart, ContentType is defined => the defined charset is used (and not the default)

So I don't get your point. Where is your difficulty/problem?
I withdraw my last comment about the content-type and charset in multipart requests: It's covered by #1332

I've looked to the issue on attribute name and filename in HttpPostRequestEncoder/Decoder.

While I finished the change, I run (V3 only since V4 is not functional for another issue) the upload test. And guess what? It does not work anymore because of the lack of URI encoding. How could it be?

Well, you pass as argument a value with "not legal" characters as in HTML unescaped, then the parser will be broken on the opposite side. The example could be seen in "secondinfo" parameter ending with an extra '&', which is ok if URIencoded, but not if not escaped.

So what could be done is to allow name only to be "as is", but not value. Therefore, the filename of a file transmitted through HTTP should be escaped (as it is a value) and unescaped on the opposite side.

Did I missed something?

Hmm, even the name should be escaped, since it will break also the parser if not correctly written on application side... So I guess this issue could not be fixed...

Am I right or did I missed sometheing?

However I found out that some cases where not taking correctly into account (and therefore not decoding properly), so the issue probably... But still the name and value seem to need to be URI escaped.

For issue #1313, partial fix: enhance coding/deconding to missing part.
Now filename is correctly undecoded. 
Name and Value must be encoded to allow parsing and respect to HTTP RFC since all value and name must be URI encoded (and then decoded). Some items were not correctly decoded, so the reason of the issue.

For issue #1332, add text/plain to content-type as default type if not specified.

I tested https://github.com/netty/netty/tree/3 and it is not working as I need it. I still think that name and filename must not be URL escaped in multipart requests. I don't know if Firefox is doing it according to the spec. But whatever they do, is certainly the de facto standard. So I tested this little HTML form: ``` html Multipart/form-data

Multipart/form-data

``` And this is the request that Firefox created, when clicking on `submit`: ``` text POST /multipart HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; rv:20.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/20.0 Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8 Accept-Language: en-us,de-de;q=0.8,de;q=0.5,en;q=0.3 Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate Connection: keep-alive Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=---------------------------106031242222620 Content-Length: 568 -----------------------------106031242222620 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="foo bar" space -----------------------------106031242222620 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="foo$bar" dollar -----------------------------106031242222620 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="foo+bar" plus -----------------------------106031242222620 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="foo\"bar" quote -----------------------------106031242222620 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="foo&bar" ampersand -----------------------------106031242222620-- ``` Please note that only the double quotes are escaped. But only with a backslash, not with URL encoding. All other special characters, especially the ampersand, the space and the dollar are not.

OK, so only for Multipart right ?
Because for not multipart, it will break the URI answer ("&" will break the decoding).
Can you confirm this will only concern Multipart ?
